title: Green’s Theorem
lead: Green’s theorem is the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus one dimension up: a line integral around the boundary of a plane region equals a double integral over the region. This section states its circulation and flux forms, uses them for work, flux and the area enclosed by a curve, meets source-free fields and their stream functions, and extends the theorem to regions with holes.
objectives: Apply the circulation form of Green’s theorem.
Apply the flux form of Green’s theorem.
Calculate circulation and flux on more general regions.
summary_html:
• Green’s theorem relates the integral over a connected region to an integral over the boundary of the region. Green’s theorem is a version of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus in one higher dimension.
  • Green’s Theorem comes in two forms: a circulation form and a flux form. In the circulation form, the integrand is $\kvecF\cdot \kvecT.$ In the flux form, the integrand is $\kvecF\cdot \kvecN.$
  • Green’s theorem can be used to transform a difficult line integral into an easier double integral, or to transform a difficult double integral into an easier line integral.
  • A vector field is source free if it has a stream function. The flux of a source-free vector field across a closed curve is zero, just as the circulation of a conservative vector field across a closed curve is zero.

(b) In this image, we see the three-level curves of g and vector field ∇g. The gradient vectors are perpendicular to the corresponding level curve. Use Green’s theorem to prove the area of a disk with radius $a$ is $A=\pi a^{2}.$

answer.solution: Let $D$ be the disk of radius $a$ about the origin and $C$ its boundary circle, oriented counterclockwise and parameterized by $x=a\cos t,$ $y=a\sin t,$ $0\le t\le 2\pi.$ The field $\textbf{F}=\langle -\frac{y}{2},\frac{x}{2}\rangle$ has $Q_{x}-P_{y}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=1,$ so by Green’s theorem $A=\iint_{D}dA=\frac{1}{2}\int_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{2\pi}(a^{2}\sin^{2}t+a^{2}\cos^{2}t)\,dt=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{2\pi}a^{2}\,dt=\pi a^{2}.$

footnotes.html: The second equation is printed $f_{x}=Q;$ since $\nabla f=\mathbf{F},$ it is $f_{y}=Q,$ which gives $f_{yy}=Q_{y}$ below.
The book prints “a potential function for $f$”; $f$ is a potential function for the field $\mathbf{F}.$
The derivative is printed $\frac{\partial}{\partial x};$ $f_{yy}$ is $\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(e^{x}\cos y)=-e^{x}\sin y.$

Here and in the computation below, $\int_{C}$ stands for the flux across the clockwise triangle $S,$ and the computation’s first line is printed without its minus sign: $\int_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{N}\,ds=-\int_{-S}\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{N}\,ds=-\iint_{D}(P_{x}+Q_{y})\,dA,$ as the next line has it.
